sections.html:
The Lake County seat sits in northwest Indiana, around 40 miles southeast of the Chicago Loop, and spreads over roughly 18 square miles. Population was 33,899 in 2020 and is estimated at 35,616 now. Homeowners dominate: 85.5% of housing is owner-occupied, owner-occupied homes have a median value of $294,800, and rent runs a median $1,485.

Few rentals means a worn-out house is easy to spot next to its neighbors. Mortgage-backed buyers tend to demand repairs before closing, so owners with dated kitchens or old roofs often turn to an as-is cash sale instead.

Interstate 65 serves the city, and Chicago is about 40 miles away. Commuters can also reach the South Shore Line at the Munster/Dyer South Shore station, and some residents use the Gary Metro Center and East Chicago stations. Gary Public Transportation Corporation runs buses along the 93rd Avenue corridor.

The Crown Point Sportsplex, a 95-acre outdoor sports complex off I-65, and the Lake County Fairgrounds are local draws. When you describe your house to a buyer, a short drive to the interstate and the rail stations is worth stating plainly. Distance to Chicago helps a listing, but it does not change what a roof or furnace costs to replace.

sections.h2: Which school district is the house in?
sections.html:
The city is split between Center and Ross townships, and each has its own public school corporation: Crown Point Community School Corporation for Center, Merrillville Community School Corporation for Ross.

Families shopping for a house ask this first. Only your property address settles it, so look it up before you talk with any buyer.

The city has three historic districts: Courthouse Square, Sunnyside and Holley. A house in one may face design review for exterior work. The state seller form asks if your lot sits in a locally designated district, so you need a firm answer before signing it.

Unsure about your street? Ask the city before completing the form.

sections.h2: Recording a deed and the sale paperwork
sections.html:
Your deed gets filed at the Lake County Recorder's office, the same counter that takes mortgages, liens and releases. Find it on the second floor of Building A at 2293 N. Main Street, Crown Point. Weekday hours run 8:30 am to 4:30 pm, and you can reach staff at 219-755-3730.

Every residential transfer also needs a sales disclosure form filed with the deed. The statute leaves out a few documents, such as mortgages, short leases and certain quitclaim deeds. In practice the closing company fills the form out when it prepares the deed, so you rarely do it yourself.

Most sellers also complete the state's owner disclosure form. Questions touch the foundation, roof, structure, mechanical systems, water and sewer, meth contamination, any flood plain knowledge and historic district status. Selling as-is does not excuse you from it, and the buyer still receives a copy, so answer truthfully.

  • Request a payoff letter if a mortgage is open.
  • Confirm your township and school corporation.
  • Ask the Lake County Treasurer whether any tax is unpaid.
  • Pick the closing company.

Lake County homeowners pay in two halves. The statute, Indiana Code 6-1.1-22-9, puts them on May 10 and November 10, though the state's own calendar nudges a date by a day when it falls on a weekend. Pay within 30 days after the deadline and you add a 5% penalty. Wait longer than that and the penalty is 10%.

Send payment to the Lake County Treasurer. The office shares the Main Street address in Crown Point, and its phone is 219-755-3760.

Taxes left unpaid can put a parcel into the county's tax sale. The delinquent list is built by July 1 or 51 days after the due date, whichever applies. A sale charge is added, certified letters go out, and owner names run in two local newspapers. Bidding happens online, and no bid can be lower than everything owed on the parcel. Questions about redeeming go to the Auditor at 219-755-3155.

Behind on taxes and thinking of selling? Letting closing proceeds cover the balance is a common fix, ideally before the list is certified. Mention the debt to the title company up front so the payoff number is waiting when you need it. A cash sale can move fast enough to beat that deadline when a listing could not.

sections.h2: How a cash sale runs, step by step
sections.html:
It is a short path. Call or write with the address and a rough description of condition. We walk through the house and put a written offer in front of you. Say yes, and a title company opens a file, searches the title and drafts the deed. The closing date is yours to choose, and funds are paid at the table.

Because no bank is involved, no appraisal or loan approval can collapse in the final week. Nothing in the house has to be fixed first. The roof, the furnace and the dated kitchen stay exactly as they are.

Before you call, it helps to gather a few things:

  • Your latest tax statement, or the balance the Treasurer shows.
  • The payoff figure from your lender, if there is a loan.
  • Any code or insurance letters about the house.
  • Every name on the title, including heirs when an owner has died.
  • Your keys and a list of anything you plan to leave behind.

When an estate owns the house, the personal representative signs the deed and the court paperwork must be in order first. Begin the probate talk early. That step, more than the buyer, usually sets the timeline.

sections.h2: Who sells to a cash buyer here?
sections.html:
Most owners here have built up real equity, so what pushes them to sell is time, repair costs or an estate. Typical cases:

  • A parent's house in Lake County that has to clear probate before anyone can sell it.
  • A property with an aging roof, furnace or foundation that an inspector would flag.
  • A landlord leaving a rental, which is unusual in a town where most owners live in their homes.
  • A family moving away that cannot pay two mortgages while a listing sits.

A cash offer skips the appraisal and the repair haggling. It will typically land below a fully renovated retail sale, so measure it against what a listing would net after commission, repairs and months of carrying costs. Ask for the terms in writing.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed for a Crown Point house?
faqs.a: At the Lake County Recorder, on the second floor of Building A, 2293 N. Main Street. Call 219-755-3730 to confirm weekday hours.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due in Crown Point?
faqs.a: Half is due each May 10 and November 10, shifting a day when that lands on a weekend. Late by up to 30 days costs 5%, and later than that costs 10%.

faqs.q: Which school district is my Crown Point house in?
faqs.a: That follows the township. Center Township homes belong to the Crown Point corporation, and Ross Township homes belong to Merrillville.

faqs.q: Do I need to fill out a disclosure form to sell my Crown Point home?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. The state form asks you about the roof, foundation, systems, water and sewer, meth contamination, flood plain and historic district. Your closing company can tell you if an exemption fits your sale.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Crown Point house with back taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The balance is typically paid out of your proceeds at closing. Waiting too long can land the parcel in the online county tax sale, so move early.
